*You can never look at the data too much.* -- Mark Engerman

The world confronts us. Make decisions we must.

We do all of our data science in the cloud, using GitHub Codespaces with Visual Studio Code (VS Code).

In this chapter you will sign up for GitHub, create a Codespace, and answer questions along the way, all right here on this page, powered by **[learnr2](https://ppbds.github.io/learnr2/)**. Everything runs in your browser. 

Your answers to the questions on this page save automatically in your browser, so you can close the page and come back later without losing anything. If you ever want to wipe them all and begin again, click the **Start Over** button in the right-hand sidebar, below the table of contents. 

Start by telling us who you are. Your instructor might also ask you to fill in the "ID" field so that your work can be matched to a grading database. If not, leave the "ID" field blank. Fill in the fields below and click **Submit**. You can edit your answers. 

```{r}
#| label: student-information-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::student_info()
```

## How to take a screenshot {.unnumbered}

Many questions in this chapter ask you to paste a screenshot as proof that you did something. Take the screenshot first, then click into the question's answer box and paste it with `Ctrl + V` (Windows, Chromebook) or `Cmd + V` (Mac). There is no upload button. A preview of your screenshot appears in the box when it has worked. Then click **Submit Answer**.

The easiest way to acccomplsh this is to copy the screenshot to your clipboard, so that you can paste it right away:

* **Windows:** press `Windows + Shift + S`, then drag a box around what you want to capture. The screenshot is copied to your clipboard.

* **Mac:** press `Cmd + Control + Shift + 4`, then drag a box around what you want to capture. Adding `Control` is what copies the screenshot to your clipboard. Without it, `Cmd + Shift + 4` saves a file to your Desktop instead, which you cannot paste.

* **Chromebook:** press `Ctrl + Shift + Show windows` (the key with a rectangle and two lines on it), drag a box around what you want to capture, and click **Copy to clipboard** in the notification that appears.

The screenshot should capture enough that we can confirm that you followed our instructions.

## Use either Chrome or Edge {.unnumbered}

In theory, the below instructions work in any browser. In practice, we have found that the best experience is with either Chrome or Edge. If you are not using either Chrome or Edge, then install one of them now: [Chrome](https://www.google.com/chrome/) or [Edge](https://explore.microsoft.com/en-us/edge/download). We recommend Chrome.

Once you have Chrome (or Edge) installed, start it. Paste a screenshot of it below. Make sure that the screenshot includes the name of the browser, probably best captured from the menu.

Your screenshot should look similar to this.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/chrome-new-tab-example.png")
```

## GitHub {.unnumbered}

Click [here](https://github.com/) and sign up for a GitHub by using the green button. Use your school email address for this account, if you are a student. 

Useful [advice](https://happygitwithr.com/github-acct.html#username-advice) for choosing a username includes using your real name, so people know who they are dealing with and can guess or remember it easily; making sure it is something you would be comfortable showing a future boss; keeping it short, and making it as unique as possible in as few characters as you can. Finally, make it timeless by avoiding references to your current university, employer, or home town. 

Once you have signed up and are signed in, go to `github.com/` followed by your username, and click the **Overview** tab. Your screenshot should look similar to this.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "A screenshot of a GitHub profile page in a browser, on the Overview tab, with the address bar showing github.com followed by the username."
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/github-profile-example.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: github-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste a screenshot of the Overview tab of your GitHub profile, at github.com/[your username]. Make sure the address bar is visible.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE
)
```

The [GitHub Student Developer Pack](https://education.github.com/pack) provides all sorts of perks, but you must visit that page to turn on the benefits. It confirms your student status on the basis of you having an email account at your school. 

If you are a student, go to that page now, sign in, and apply for the benefits. When you finish, GitHub tells you that your application has been submitted. Your screenshot should look similar to this. (If you are not a student, skip this question.)

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "A screenshot of GitHub's Education Benefits Application dialog with a green message reading: Your application has been submitted."
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/student-pack-submitted-example.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: github-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste a screenshot of the message from GitHub saying that your Education Benefits Application has been submitted.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE
)
```

On GitHub, your projects are organized into "repositories," usually called "repos."

GitHub gives every account 60 free Codespaces hours per month. Free hours are not infinite, however, so it is your responsibility to stop (and delete) Codespaces you are no longer using.

Go to [`https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter).

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/cs-1.png")
```

This Codespace is for learning the platform, not for your permanent work.

Click the green **Code** button at the top right of the repository page, switch to the **Codespaces** tab, and click **"Create codespace on main."**


GitHub gives your Codespace a randomly generated name. Mine is "ominous space adventure", but yours will be different. The red arrows in the example below point to the four places where that name appears: the address bar of your browser, the box at the top center of VS Code, the top of the Explorer panel on the left, and the blue button at the bottom left.

### Touring the workspace {.unnumbered}

VS Code is an integrated development environment (IDE) for coding and data science. Highlights:

* This Codespace is in the cloud. The URL will be a combination of the GitHub-determined human-readable but somewhat nonsensical name — `ominous space adventure` in my case — and a bunch of letters and numbers. There is no need to remember this URL. GitHub keeps track of things. You can see all your current Codespaces at [`https://github.com/codespaces`](https://github.com/codespaces).

* In the upper right-hand corner are the "Customize Layout ..." buttons. These are part of the VS Code "Title Bar." Since we aren't using the AI tools right now, it often makes sense to close the "Chat" window, which appears on the right side of the screen. You can close this in two ways: Click the "X" mark or click the "Toggle Secondary Side Bar" button, the furthest right-hand button. You can then bring the Chat window back by clicking the "Toggle Secondary Side Bar" button again. Try it now.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/chat-buttons-cs.png")
```

* The "Activity Bar" is the narrow vertical strip on the far left with icons for Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions, etc. By default, the "Explorer" button is selected, showing that the only thing in the project is a folder called `.devcontainer`. Click on that folder to show its contents.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/cs-4.png")
```

Click on the `STUDENT_WORKFLOW.md` file. Doing so opens that file in the Editor window. Your screen should now look like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/cs-4b.png")
```

The "Editor" is the large central area where you edit files.

The "Panel" is the horizontal area below the Editor, containing the Problems, Output, Debug Console, Terminal, and Ports views. Our main focus is the Terminal view. This is where we "talk" to both the (cloud) computer itself and to the R program that it provides.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/cs-5.png")
```

 The Terminal view currently shows two terminals. They are listed along the right-hand side. You can move back and forth between them by clicking on them. You can close a terminal by clicking on the trash can icon next to its name, which appears when you hover your cursor over the name.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/t1.png")
```

* You can start new bash Terminals by clicking on the `+` sign above the list of terminals. Do so now.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/t2.png")
```

The language can be a little confusing. There is a capital T "Terminal" view, which is one of the tabs across the top of the Panel. In that Terminal view, we can work with many individual small T "terminals" of various sorts. So far, you have only seen bash Terminals, which get a capital T because they are a type of named terminal. The bash shell is a program that lets you "talk" to the computer itself.

In addition to bash Terminals, we can also start an R session under the Terminal. Instead of clicking the `+` sign, click the small downward-pointing arrow next to it. This will show a variety of options.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/cs-6.png")
```

Select "R Terminal." This will start an R session that lets you "talk" to R in the same way that a bash shell allows you to talk to the computer.

Click on the "R Interactive" tab which should appear beneath the other terminals on the right side of the Panel.

Type in `2 + 2` at the R prompt and hit `enter` (Windows) or `return` (Mac). (Going forward we will just use `Enter` to refer to this action. Mac users should hit `return`.)

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/t3.png")
```

An IDE like VS Code is designed to organize all the different work we do as data scientists. We need to talk to the computer via the bash Terminal (a terminal running the bash shell), talk to R, view plots, and so on.

### The Getting Started exercises {.unnumbered}

The exercises below run directly on this page, powered by **[learnr2](https://ppbds.github.io/learnr2/)**, so you do not need to launch anything inside your Codespace. Keep your Codespace open in another window -- you will switch back to its bash Terminal for one of the exercises below.

#### Introduction {.unnumbered}

This chapter teaches you how tutorials work. There are only three steps: tell us who you are (which you did at the top of this page), run a command in a Terminal and copy the result, and download a copy of your answers. It should take about five minutes. Every tutorial you complete after this chapter uses the same sequence.

#### The bash Terminal {.unnumbered}

Tutorials include exercises. Most exercises ask you to run a command in a terminal and then copy the result into the answer box below. You will do that once now.

Look at the bottom of your VS Code window. The horizontal area below the editor is called the "Panel." The red arrow below points to the new-terminal plus button (`+`) on the right side of the Panel.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/get-bash.png")
```

Press `+`. This opens a new **bash** Terminal -- the text-based interface in which you type commands to tell your Codespace what to do. The pattern is always the same: you send a command, the terminal executes it, and it gives you something back.

##### Exercise 1 {.unnumbered}

Click into the bash Terminal, type `pwd`, and then press `Enter`. To "run" a command means to type it and then press this key.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/pwd.png")
```

**Do not just type the command into the answer box!** You must run the command in the bash Terminal and then copy the result.

**C**opy and **P**aste both the **C**ommand *and* the **R**esponse from the bash Terminal into the box below. We abbreviate this instruction throughout the book as **CP**/**CR**.

```{r}
#| label: the-getting-started-exercises-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste, into the box below, both the command you ran and the response the Terminal printed.",
  type = "reflection_editable"
)
```

We typically provide example answers, like the one below, after you submit your own response. Do not be concerned if your answer differs from the example we show.

````
codespace-starter $ pwd
/workspaces/codespace-starter
codespace-starter $
````

`pwd` stands for **p**rint **w**orking **d**irectory: it shows the directory in which the terminal is working. The response confirms that you are inside your Codespace, a complete computer running in the cloud. It is OK if your formatting differs from ours. What matters is that you show that you ran the command as instructed.

That is the usual process: run something in a terminal, copy the command and the response, paste them into the answer box. Almost every exercise in every later tutorial works this way.

##### Exercise 2 {.unnumbered}

Every answer on this page, including the one you just gave, is saved to your browser as you go -- not only once you finally download your work. Reload this page right now to see for yourself: your name, email, and the answer above should all still be there, exactly as you left them.

There is no R session running in your Codespace for this chapter -- your answers live in your browser, not on a server, so nothing about your Codespace needs to stay open for your progress to be safe. There is also a "Start Over" button at the bottom of the sidebar if you ever want to clear your answers and begin again, which only acts after you confirm.

#### Your answers {.unnumbered}

At the end of every tutorial, you download a copy of your answers, and you do the same here. First, answer the question below about how many minutes you spent on this chapter. Then click the button below that to gather every answer on this page into a single file and download it.

```{r}
#| label: the-getting-started-exercises-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "How many minutes, approximately, did it take you to complete this

```

```{r}
#| label: the-getting-started-exercises-3
```

After clicking the "Download My Answers" button, you will be prompted to save a file whose name starts with `getting-started-2`, followed by a timestamp. By default, this file will be saved in the `Downloads` folder on your computer. This action only downloads the file; it does not send the file to anyone.

Unless your instructor tells you otherwise, send them this file as-is (for example, attached to an email or uploaded to your course's learning management system).

### Stopping, restarting and deleting the Codespace {.unnumbered}

A Codespace is your responsibility in the same way that your laptop is your responsibility. While a Codespace is running it counts against your free hours, and an unused Codespace will be deleted by GitHub after 30 days.

There are three common ways to close a Codespace.

First, just leave it alone. GitHub will close it on its own after 30 minutes of inactivity, though we recommend changing that default to 15 minutes in your [Codespaces settings](https://github.com/settings/codespaces).

Second, type `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P`. The Command Palette provides access to all VS Code commands. Type `stop` into the search bar.

On some browsers, the keyboard shortcut does not work. You can always access the Command Palette by clicking the search bar at the top of the window and typing `>` followed by key words from the command you would like to use.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/command-palette.png")
```

Select "Codespaces: Stop Current Codespace."

Third, you can go to your personal Codespaces control panel at [`https://github.com/codespaces`](https://github.com/codespaces). You can also reach this page from any page on GitHub by clicking the menu icon in the upper left and selecting "Codespaces":

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/t7.png")
```

Which brings up this lst of options. Select "Codespaces."

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/t8.png")
```

Your main Codespaces page should look something like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/codespaces-1.png")
```

This shows all your Codespaces, both active and inactive. The `...` menu on each row provides several commands, including "Stop Codespace."

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/codespaces-2.png")
```

Simply closing the browser window *does not* stop your Codespace from running. Always stop a Codespace explicitly to preserve your free hours.

Now stop this Codespace using whichever method you prefer.

Once it is stopped, you can restart it from your [Codespaces page](https://github.com/codespaces) by clicking the `...` menu next to this Codespace and then selecting **Open in Browser**.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/codespaces-3.png")
```

Once you are done with a Codespace, you should **delete it.** To do so, go to your [Codespaces page](https://github.com/codespaces), click the `...` menu next to this Codespace and select **Delete**.

This Codespace was a sandbox. You do not own [`PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter), so there is nowhere for your work to go once you stop using the Codespace. That is fine — you have already downloaded your answers, which is the only thing here worth keeping.

```{r}
#| label: stopping-restarting-and-deleting-the-codespace-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste a screenshot of your Codespaces control panel (https://github.com/codespaces) showing this Codespace stopped, or already deleted.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE
)
```

## Using your own machine

You can do all of this work on your own laptop, if you prefer. But, in that case, you are responsible for setting everything up. That means installing VS Code, Git and R. You will almost certainly want to install the same VS Code extensions which we use, including:

```
"reditorsupport.r",
"quarto.quarto",
"PPBDS.vscode-r-tutorials",
"ritwickdey.LiveServer",
"tomoki1207.pdf",
"mechatroner.rainbow-csv"x
```

This listing is from  the `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` file from [`PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter). You may also find it useful to use the same VS settings which are defined there.

You will also need to install, by hand, various R packages. From the R Terminal, you would run commands like:

```
install.packages("pak")
```

You may be asked to select a CRAN mirror. It does not matter which you choose.

```
pak::pak("tidyverse")
pak::pak("PPBDS/vscode.tutorials")
```

These steps are not enough to perfectly replicate what we show in the Codespace. See `PPBDS/devcontainers` for more details.

But this should be enough to get you started, should you decide to go this route. If you have trouble, ask AI, pointing it toward this chapter and to the [`PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter) and `PPBDS/devcontainers` repos.

## A second GitHub account {.unnumbered}

Create a second GitHub account by following the same instructions as in the [GitHub](#github) section above. Name it the same as your first account, with `-tutorials` added to the end. If your first username is `john-doe`, your second one is `john-doe-tutorials`.

GitHub requires a different email address for each account, so you cannot reuse the one you gave your first account.

```{r}
#| label: a-second-github-account-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Go to your new account's profile page, github.com/ followed by your new username, and paste a screenshot of it below. Make sure the address bar is visible, so that the full username (ending in -tutorials) shows in the screenshot.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE
)
```

## Start a tutorial {.unnumbered}

You will do most of your work in tutorials like the one you are about to start. This section shows you how to start one. That is all you need to know: the tutorial itself asks for your name and email, helps you download your answers, and so on.

Sign in to GitHub with your second account, the one ending in `-tutorials`. Go to [`https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter) and create a Codespace, exactly as you did in the "Launching the Codespace" section above.

Once your Codespace is ready, look at the Activity Bar, the narrow vertical strip of icons on the far left. Hover over the icons until you find the one labeled **R Tutorials**, near the bottom, and click it. This lists the R packages that have tutorials. Click the package named **[vscode.tutorials](https://ppbds.github.io/vscode.tutorials/)** to see its tutorials.

Find the tutorial named **Orientation**. Hover over its name and click the rightward-pointing arrow that appears. Doing so starts the tutorial, which takes a minute or so. A new terminal named "R Tutorial" appears in the Panel, and the tutorial then offers to open in your browser. Accept that offer. If you miss it, hover over the web address in the "R Tutorial" terminal and press `Cmd + Click` (Mac) or `Ctrl + Click` (Windows, Chromebook).

```{r}
#| label: start-a-tutorial-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Open the Orientation tutorial in your browser and paste a screenshot of its first page below. Make sure the address bar is visible in the screenshot.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE
)
```

You do not need to finish the Orientation tutorial now. When you are done with this Codespace, stop it and delete it, as described in the "Stopping, restarting and deleting the Codespace" section above.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

You should have done the following:

- Signed up for a GitHub account.
- Signed up for a second GitHub account, named like your first one with `-tutorials` added to the end.
- Used your second account to start the **Orientation** tutorial from **[vscode.tutorials](https://ppbds.github.io/vscode.tutorials/)** in a Codespace.
- Used a throwaway Codespace on [`PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter) to complete the **Getting Started** exercises right here on this page, powered by **[learnr2](https://ppbds.github.io/learnr2/)**, downloaded your answers, then **deleted** the Codespace.

For doing some tutorials, a throwaway Codespace is all you need: complete the tutorial and download your answers --- no repository needed. When a later tutorial asks you to keep your work and build on it, the next chapter, [Git and GitHub](git-and-github.qmd), shows you how to create a repository you own.

Let's get started!

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started-2/images/ending.gif")
```
